reviewBoundary: Six newly authored complete English reading passages in three senior practices, four questions per passage. Invented venues, organisations and incidents are original narrative examples, not citations to real studies or real advertised events. Same-author review checks text evidence and every distractor. No independent teacher or learner calibration claimed.

units.title: 阅读理解 · 船馆开放日与跑步节奏

materials.title: A. River Boat Museum: family open day
materials.text:
Explore how people travelled on our river at the River Boat Museum's family open day, Sunday 18 May, 10:00-17:00. The exhibition rooms are free, but two special activities require separate bookings.

Build a paper boat
This 45-minute workshop starts at 10:30 and 14:00. Children aged seven to twelve work with an accompanying adult to build and test a paper boat. The price is six pounds per child; one accompanying adult attends free. Materials are provided. Please book online by Friday 16 May. There are twelve child places in each session. Younger children may explore the exhibition but cannot join the workshop.

Meet a boat builder
At 12:00, local builder Eva Green will explain how she chooses wood and show visitors some hand tools. The talk lasts thirty minutes and is suitable for visitors aged ten and above. It is free, but seats must be reserved by telephone. The demonstration takes place on land; it is not a boat trip.

Visiting information
Bring a packed lunch to eat in the garden, or buy sandwiches at the café. Drinks are not allowed in the exhibition rooms. The garden will close in heavy rain, but all indoor activities will continue.

Buses 4 and 9 stop outside the museum. The small car park is reserved for visitors with mobility needs. If it is full, staff can direct eligible drivers to an additional accessible space nearby. Other drivers should use the public car park beside the library, a ten-minute walk away. Dogs are welcome in the garden but only assistance dogs may enter the building.

questions.prompt: What is required for a child to join the paper-boat workshop?
options: Bringing their own paper and tools.
Being at least ten years old.
Attending with an adult and booking online.
Reserving a place by telephone on Sunday.
questions.explanation: Seven-to-twelve-year-olds attend with an adult and book online by Friday. Materials are supplied; ten is the talk's minimum age; telephone booking belongs to the talk, not Sunday workshop registration.

questions.prompt: How much does one adult with two eligible children pay for the workshop?
options: Six pounds.
Twelve pounds.
Eighteen pounds.
Nothing.
questions.explanation: Two child places at six pounds total twelve; one accompanying adult is free. Six counts only one child, eighteen incorrectly charges the adult, and free confuses exhibition admission with the paid workshop.

questions.prompt: What can visitors expect at Eva Green's activity?
options: A trip along the river in a wooden boat.
A chance to build a full-size boat.
A talk that requires no advance reservation.
A land-based explanation with hand-tool demonstrations.
questions.explanation: Eva explains wood choice and demonstrates tools on land, with reserved seats. The text explicitly rules out a boat trip; full-size construction and unreserved attendance are not offered.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct about visiting arrangements?
options: Most drivers should park near the library.
Heavy rain will cancel every activity.
All dogs may enter the exhibition rooms.
Visitors must buy lunch from the café.
questions.explanation: Drivers without mobility needs use the library-side public car park. Indoor activities continue in rain; only assistance dogs enter; packed lunches are permitted.

materials.title: B. One more lap
materials.text:
On my first evening with the neighbourhood running group, I tried to stay beside its fastest runner. We had barely left the park gate when I began breathing hard. By the second lap, I was walking, embarrassed to see people pass me.

A woman named Nora slowed down. She asked whether I wanted company. I expected advice about moving my arms or buying better shoes. Instead, she asked me to describe the film I had watched the night before. I could produce only a few words at a time.

'Let's slow down until you can finish a sentence,' she said. At that speed, I felt almost too comfortable. Yet I kept running for the rest of the lap. When we reached the gate again, Nora asked whether I could manage another one. For the first time that evening, the answer was yes.

Over the next month, I stopped measuring each outing against the fastest person's time. I recorded how long I could run without needing to walk. Some evenings were easier than others, especially when I had slept well. Nora warned me against treating every difficult run as proof that I had made no progress.

Then the group held a friendly relay. I ran my section more quickly than I had expected. I was still far from the fastest runner, but I reached the finish with enough breath to cheer for the next person.

Nora never told me that speed did not matter. She enjoyed racing and worked hard on her own times. What she taught me was that borrowing someone else's pace was not the same as finding a useful challenge for myself. Now, when a newcomer falls behind, I slow down and ask an ordinary question. The conversation gives us something to share, and sometimes it tells us more about the right pace than a number on a watch.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer start walking on the first evening?
options: The group had reached the end of its planned route.
Nora asked everyone to stop running.
The writer's new shoes had broken.
The writer had tried to maintain an unsuitable pace.
questions.explanation: Trying to match the fastest runner left the writer breathless by lap two. The route had not ended, Nora had not stopped the group, and no broken shoes are mentioned.

questions.prompt: Why did Nora ask the writer about a film?
options: To help find a pace at which the writer could speak comfortably.
To select a film for the whole running group.
To distract the writer while she increased their speed.
To test whether the writer remembered the film's ending.
questions.explanation: She slows them until complete sentences are possible. No group film selection or memory test is involved, and she reduces rather than increases pace.

questions.prompt: How did the writer's way of judging progress change?
options: Only winning races began to count.
Every difficult evening was treated as failure.
Personal endurance became more useful than comparison with the fastest runner.
The writer stopped recording any aspect of running.
questions.explanation: The writer records continuous running time rather than matching the leader's time. Winning is not the sole goal; Nora discourages interpreting difficulty as failure; records continue.

questions.prompt: What does the writer learn from Nora?
options: Competitive runners should never train with beginners.
A useful challenge should fit the person's present ability.
Conversation is always more accurate than every measuring device.
Speed has no value in any form of running.
questions.explanation: The main lesson is finding an appropriate personal pace. A contradicts Nora's support; C turns 'sometimes' into an absolute; D ignores Nora's enjoyment of racing and work on times.

units.title: 阅读理解 · 舞台声响与循环包装

materials.title: A. The sound of an empty room
materials.text:
At a workshop for young theatre makers, sound designer Imani asked everyone to remain silent for thirty seconds. Most participants initially heard nothing. Then they began to notice a ventilation fan, a distant door and the movement of someone adjusting a chair. The room had not become noisier. Their attention had changed.

Imani was preparing them to record dialogue for a short performance. Several students had assumed that the main challenge would be speaking clearly. That mattered, she agreed, but a recording also preserved sounds that people could easily ignore while concentrating on a conversation. A voice could be understandable in the room and still be difficult to hear in the recording.

The group tried recording one scene near the window and another farther inside. The second position reduced traffic noise, but it brought the actors closer to the ventilation fan. Moving away from one source did not automatically improve the whole recording. They listened to both attempts through headphones before choosing a position between the two.

Next, Imani asked the actors to leave the room while the equipment recorded its ordinary background sound. One student wondered why they needed a recording without a performance. Imani explained that short pieces of it could help join separately recorded lines, so that an edit would not jump abruptly from a room's background noise to complete digital silence. It was a tool for consistency, not an attempt to make the performance louder.

By the end, the students had not found a perfectly silent location. They had identified the sounds they could control, moved a loose chair and chosen a time when the corridor was quieter. They also understood why listening to a test mattered more than assuming a place would work because it felt quiet. For Imani, good preparation began with hearing what a room was already doing, before asking it to become the setting for something else.

questions.prompt: What was the purpose of the opening silence?
options: To prove the room contained no background sound.
To draw attention to sounds participants had initially overlooked.
To persuade students not to record any dialogue.
To measure how loudly each actor could speak.
questions.explanation: The silence changes attention and reveals fan, door and chair sounds. A denies those sounds; C contradicts the recording workshop; D confuses background listening with vocal testing.

questions.prompt: What did the two recording positions demonstrate?
options: Traffic noise disappeared whenever a window was closed.
The loudest location always produced the clearest recording.
Reducing one noise could increase exposure to another.
Headphones prevented the fan from entering a recording.
questions.explanation: The interior position reduces traffic but increases fan proximity. No closed-window test occurs; loudness is not the selection rule; headphones reveal recorded sound rather than remove it.

questions.prompt: Why was the ordinary sound of the empty room recorded?
options: To help edited dialogue retain a consistent background.
To replace all the actors' spoken lines.
To increase the loudness of every performance.
To document a complete absence of noise.
questions.explanation: Background pieces bridge edits between lines instead of jumping to digital silence. They do not replace speech, aim at increased loudness or represent a noiseless room.

questions.prompt: Which approach does Imani recommend?
options: Trusting a location as long as it feels quiet.
Postponing every recording until perfect silence is possible.
Controlling every sound throughout the entire building.
Using test recordings to make practical choices about the environment.
questions.explanation: The group tests, listens and controls manageable sources and timing. A is explicitly questioned; B is contradicted by proceeding without perfection; C exceeds the limited practical changes made.

materials.title: B. A box's second journey
materials.text:
When the small delivery company Loop Lane introduced reusable boxes, its first advertisement showed a single box making journey after journey. Customers liked the idea. Yet the operations manager, Ellis, was less interested in how often a box could theoretically be reused than in whether it actually came back.

At first, customers were asked to keep empty boxes until their next delivery. This worked well for people who ordered weekly. Others received deliveries only a few times a year. Their boxes remained under beds or in cupboards, unavailable for another journey. Loop Lane still had to buy more boxes to meet demand. A durable object sitting unused was not doing the work shown in the advertisement.

The company added return points at two neighbourhood shops. Returns increased, but so did a different kind of journey. Some customers drove to a shop solely to return a box. Ellis could not assume that every returned box represented an environmental improvement if collecting it required substantial extra travel. She encouraged customers to combine returns with trips they were already making.

Cleaning posed another question. Some boxes came back with only dry goods inside; others contained leaking food. Staff needed a procedure that protected hygiene without treating every box as if it required the most intensive cleaning. The team consulted a qualified hygiene adviser and set separate handling rules according to the condition of each return.

Ellis did not conclude that reusable packaging was a bad idea. She objected to treating 'reusable' as a complete account of how a service worked. The box's design mattered, but so did customers' routines, collection arrangements and the resources needed between uses.

Loop Lane changed its publicity. The new picture showed the return points and the cleaning stage as well as the delivery. It was a less elegant image than a single endlessly travelling box, but a more useful description of the system the company was trying to build.

questions.prompt: What was Ellis's main concern about the original advertisement?
options: It showed boxes that were too small for customers' orders.
It gave too much detail about the cleaning process.
It assumed possible reuse would translate into actual repeated use.
It discouraged people from ordering weekly deliveries.
questions.explanation: The distinction is theoretical durability versus boxes actually returning. Size, excessive cleaning detail and discouragement of weekly ordering are not her objections.

questions.prompt: Why were extra boxes still needed in the early scheme?
options: All returned boxes were immediately thrown away.
Customers were forbidden to order more than once a year.
The boxes broke before completing their first delivery.
Many boxes waited a long time with infrequent customers.
questions.explanation: Infrequent orders kept boxes in homes instead of circulation. Disposal, an ordering ban and immediate breakage are not stated.

questions.prompt: What complication followed the introduction of return points?
options: Some people made additional car journeys just to return boxes.
The two shops stopped selling their usual goods.
Customers could no longer return boxes during other trips.
The company abandoned all hygiene requirements.
questions.explanation: Some dedicated return drives create extra travel. The shops' stock is not discussed; combined trips are encouraged, not prohibited; hygiene rules are strengthened with advice.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the passage?
options: Durability alone guarantees that packaging reduces resource use.
The value of reusable packaging depends on the wider operating system.
Reusable boxes should be replaced by new boxes after every delivery.
Advertising should avoid showing any complicated process.
questions.explanation: Returns, travel, cleaning and routines determine actual operation alongside design. A is the inadequate assumption challenged; C contradicts continued reuse; D contradicts the expanded publicity.

units.title: 阅读理解 · 修复照片与连载故事

materials.title: A. The missing corner
materials.text:
A community history group wanted to display an old photograph of a street parade. The surviving print had a pale strip across one corner, where part of the crowd had faded almost completely. A volunteer used editing software to fill the space with figures resembling those elsewhere in the picture. At normal viewing size, the result looked convincing. The difficulty was deciding what kind of object the group now possessed.

The volunteer had not discovered the missing spectators. She had produced a plausible arrangement from the surviving image. That distinction mattered because the group planned to use the photograph as evidence about who had attended the parade. A reconstructed face could easily acquire a historical identity that the original print did not support. Technical smoothness might make an uncertain claim harder, rather than easier, to notice.

The group considered keeping the altered image but adding a small note. Some members worried that a note beneath the frame would be lost whenever someone copied the image for another purpose. Others argued that showing only the damaged print would prevent viewers from understanding the atmosphere of the scene. Neither concern was unreasonable, but they addressed different aims: preserving evidence and helping people imagine an event.

The final display placed two images side by side. One was a carefully scanned copy of the surviving print, with the faded area visible. The other was labelled as a modern reconstruction, and the restored corner was outlined. The group also retained the original scan and a record of each alteration. Viewers could enjoy the proposed appearance without being asked to mistake it for a newly recovered fact.

This solution did not make every restoration question simple. Increasing contrast can reveal a detail already present; replacing a missing face supplies something absent. Between those examples lie many decisions requiring judgment. What the display established was a habit of describing interventions in relation to the claim an image would support. A restored picture can have value, but that value need not depend on allowing its additions to disappear from view.

questions.prompt: What was the central problem with the volunteer's edited image?
options: It failed to reproduce the crowd's clothing consistently.
It might present plausible additions as historical evidence.
It could not be viewed at an ordinary display size.
It revealed previously invisible identities with certainty.
questions.explanation: Invented plausible figures could be mistaken for recovered spectators. A and C contradict its convincing appearance; D is precisely the unsupported certainty at risk, not an actual discovery.

questions.prompt: Why did some members consider a small explanatory note inadequate?
options: They believed no visitor would ever read any label.
The editing software could not produce printed text.
The image might circulate separately from its explanation.
The photograph would have to remain in permanent storage.
questions.explanation: Copies could lose the note below the frame. A exaggerates a circulation concern into a universal claim; B invents a software limitation; D invents an access restriction.

questions.prompt: What did the two-image display allow viewers to do?
options: Compare surviving evidence with an explicitly identified reconstruction.
Determine the names of every person in the original crowd.
Treat both images as unaltered records of the parade.
See the original print without any visible damage.
questions.explanation: The damaged scan and outlined reconstruction separate evidence from interpretation. The display cannot establish all names, does not label both unaltered, and preserves visible fading in the first image.

questions.prompt: What position does the author take on restoration?
options: All adjustments to old images should be prohibited.
An attractive result removes the need to explain alterations.
Every software adjustment is equivalent to inventing a face.
Interventions should be made visible in light of the claims being made.
questions.explanation: The conclusion calls for describing interventions relative to intended claims. A rejects useful restoration more broadly than the text; B reverses the transparency principle; C ignores the contrast between revealing existing detail and adding absent content.

materials.title: B. Waiting for the next chapter
materials.text:
During a literature course, our class read a novel in weekly instalments. We were used to choosing our own reading speed, and several students disliked being asked to stop at a particular chapter. They argued that the restriction interrupted their involvement in the story. Our tutor suspected that it might also make a familiar part of reading newly noticeable: the work done by expectation.

After the first instalment, we each wrote down what we thought would happen next and identified a detail supporting the prediction. At the following meeting, some predictions proved accurate and others collapsed. What interested the tutor was not our success rate. It was the way a detail that had seemed minor could gain importance while we waited, or lose it when the narrative moved elsewhere.

Discussion changed too. When everyone had read the whole book, a confident student could organise an account around the ending, making early clues seem as though they had always pointed inevitably towards it. Reading in stages prevented us from borrowing that certainty. We had to discuss what the text made available at that moment, before later events reorganised our understanding.

The weekly pauses did not automatically produce better interpretation. A few students became so attached to their predictions that they overlooked contrary evidence. The tutor asked them to preserve their original notes, then add a second account explaining what had changed their minds. Revising a prediction was treated as an act of reading, not an admission that the first response had been worthless.

By the final chapter, I was eager to read the novel again without stopping. The course had not persuaded me that every book should be delivered in pieces. It had shown me that pace affects the questions a reader can ask. Continuous reading could reveal patterns across the whole story; waiting could expose the uncertainty through which those patterns were first encountered. Our last discussion used both perspectives. We could talk about where the novel ended without pretending that this was the only destination we had ever imagined for it.

questions.prompt: What did the tutor hope the weekly reading schedule would reveal?
options: That students should never choose their own reading speed.
That a novel's ending has no effect on its meaning.
How expectation contributes to the reading experience.
How many chapters each student could memorise.
questions.explanation: The tutor wants to make expectation visible. A turns a limited classroom method into a universal rule; B contradicts later reorganisation by endings; D introduces memorisation instead of interpretation.

questions.prompt: Why was prediction accuracy not the tutor's main interest?
options: The novel had several officially correct endings.
Students were forbidden to cite textual details.
All predictions were equally well supported by the text.
Changing expectations showed how the significance of details developed.
questions.explanation: The exercise traces details gaining or losing importance. The passage supplies no multiple endings, explicitly requires supporting details, and does not claim equal support for all predictions.

questions.prompt: What tendency did reading in stages help the class avoid?
options: Treating early evidence as if the ending had always been certain.
Discussing the story before understanding every word.
Recognising that a text may permit different expectations.
Keeping written notes of their first reactions.
questions.explanation: Staged reading prevents retrospective certainty borrowed from the known ending. B is not discussed; C is encouraged rather than avoided; D conflicts with the preserved notes.

questions.prompt: What does the writer conclude about the two reading approaches?
options: Interrupted reading should replace continuous reading in every course.
They can reveal complementary aspects of the same work.
Reading continuously makes thoughtful interpretation impossible.
Only first impressions are worth discussing after the ending.
questions.explanation: The last discussion combines whole-story patterns with uncertainty during first encounters. A and C impose absolute judgments the writer rejects; D discards the later perspective that is explicitly included.
